Part II of the volume deals with papers relatiug to the ■reorganization of the ta‘aluqas or administrative units and a •summary examination of the Jagir accounts. - Immediately on the restoration of . peace after the treaty .of Lahore, in March. 1816, the British Resident and his assistants tpok the reins of the Kh&lsa government in their, own h,ands although nominally the . Council of Regency was charge d'affaires of the State. The first thing which attracted the notice of the Resident was a want of clear, definite system in State accounts, and the many opportunities which it afforded for dishonesty and fraud. The six years of a weak and unsettled government which followed the demise of Maharaja Raujlt Singh had greatly aug- mented these chances. Besides this, the actual expenditure of government had been more than doubled during this period, although there was no substantial corresponding increase in the revenues of the country. The war (1815-16 A. D.) had caused an additional strain on the revenues and the peace that followed brought no relief. It had, rather, further reduced the permanent income of the State. The territories of Kangra and the Jalandhar Doab — the richest districts in the Sikh dominiou — were ceded to the British, and Jammu and Kashmir were •created into an independent State under Mahdraja Gulab Singh. It further involved an addition of 2 J lacs of rupees to meet the expenses of the British troops kept in the Panjab for the maintenance of peace. Such a great strain on the revenues of the country could be borne only if the finances were brought on a sounder footing by -curtailing the inflated and unnecessary expenses. The Treaty of Lahore had provided for the reduction of the Khalsa Army, and when a portion of the army was disbanded it brought about a considerable saving. The next source to draw upon was the jdgirs. These jdgirs were classed as ( i ) military, i,e., granted to the chiefs in lieu .of military service ; (n) civil, i.e., granted to the State employees in the civil depart- ment ; (in) dhannarth or religious endowments and- (iv) mis- cellaneous including th e^jfizindh mr daily allowance to in- dividuals of various description, and the inglis or pensions .allotted to the widows and relatives of certain . deceased ser- vants of the State. , The jdgirdars. sometime, retained , lands in excess of tliat-specified in, their deeds and a dhdtrmarthi or a r.ozina « ddr often continued to hold this allowance even after the

298 original sanad was cancelled. To discover these frauds a regular enquiry was instituted. The'fraudulently obtained rent-free lands were resumed along with those of the discharged members of the army. The total amount thus resumed was estimated at a little over sixteen lacs (16 lacs) per annum. Along with this, the constructive side of the work was also taken in hand. With a view to have a more definite idea of the resources of the country and of the utilizing of those resources for the benefit and the improvement of the State, the ta’aluqas were reorganized and their revenues were estimated more correctly. The accounts of the old collectors were checked and their opportunities for embezzlement very much reduced. A general Summary Settlement of each taaluqa was undertaken, and the areas of culturable lands together with the liabilities and rights of the landlords or the paying-tenants were reduced to writing.
